primary_cause: Direct company guidance cut: Q1 net revenue 2-3pp hit from COVID. Growth now 9-10% vs prior trajectory
secondary_factors: Broader risk-off selling in travel- and consumer-exposed names
store_description: On Feb. 24 Mastercard said COVID-19 would shave 2-3 points off first-quarter net revenue growth as cross-border spending weakened. The company now expected Q1 revenue growth of roughly 9-10% down from the prior trajectory. The next day's wider market selloff amplified the decline.

primary_cause: No clear Lowe's-specific catalyst. Broad cyclical/consumer selloff
secondary_factors: General concern that virus shock would hit store traffic discretionary projects and housing demand
store_description: Lowe's looks mostly like a sympathy move. By Feb. 24-25 investors were dumping consumer cyclicals as the global outbreak broadened and home-improvement retail fit the bucket of demand-sensitive domestic discretionary exposure even without a fresh company headline.

primary_cause: Macro rate shock and recession fears hurting bank earnings expectations
secondary_factors: General financial-sector de-risking. Markets pricing ~50bps Fed easing by year-end
store_description: JPM's selloff looks tied mainly to the violent move lower in Treasury yields and the market suddenly pricing aggressive Fed easing which is bad for bank net interest income and signals slower credit demand. This was bank-specific through rates and growth sensitivity but not JPM-specific through company news.

primary_cause: No clear company-specific catalyst. Global industrial-growth scare
secondary_factors: Broad de-risking in cyclical industrial names
store_description: Linde's decline fits the pattern of high-quality industrials getting sold as investors reassessed global manufacturing and capex risk. No obvious adverse Linde announcement right before the move.

primary_cause: Early market repricing of elective-procedure and hospital-utilization risk after CDC warning
secondary_factors: Broad med-tech de-risking in a falling market
store_description: This does not look like a clean company-news move. Intuitive was highly exposed to procedure volumes and once the CDC publicly warned U.S. spread was a matter of when investors started discounting the possibility of delayed elective surgeries and weaker near-term system utilization.

primary_cause: Semiconductor/tech selloff on virus fears. MWC pullout/cancellation as supporting signal
secondary_factors: Broader Nasdaq and cyclical tech weakness
store_description: Intel did not have a distinct negative corporate update right before the drop but the combination of MWC cancellation event disruption supply-chain uncertainty and concern about enterprise/PC demand made semis vulnerable.

primary_cause: No clear stock-specific catalyst. Broad tech and enterprise-spending risk repricing
secondary_factors: Legacy tech names sold off even without specific headline
store_description: IBM looks mostly like a macro/sector move. As investors rapidly repriced global growth and enterprise IT spending risk legacy tech names sold off even without a specific headline attached to the company.

primary_cause: No clear Lockheed-specific catalyst. Broad market liquidation
secondary_factors: Defense/aerospace basket selling alongside wider cyclicals
store_description: Lockheed's drop is harder to tie to a narrow headline than RTX's. No company-specific driver found so the best explanation is that it was swept into a severe index-level and sector-level risk-off move.

primary_cause: Broad semiconductor selloff on virus fears. MWC cancellation
secondary_factors: Event disruption and China demand/supply anxiety
store_description: Nvidia's drop looks mostly sectoral. The MWC cancellation and virus-related uncertainty around electronics supply chains and demand undercut semis broadly. No distinct new Nvidia headline in the 3-day window.

primary_cause: Oil-demand shock from COVID-19. Reuters: China increasing fuel exports because domestic demand slumped
secondary_factors: Broader energy-sector risk-off and recession fears
store_description: Exxon's decline is straightforward. The market was repricing a global demand hit to crude as the outbreak spread. Reuters tied the day's move directly to tumbling oil prices. China's fuel-demand weakness was a concrete supporting data point that the demand destruction was already real.

primary_cause: Smartphone/telecom ecosystem disruption from COVID-19. MWC cancellation as visible catalyst
secondary_factors: Broader handset-demand and China supply-chain fears
store_description: Qualcomm did not have a fresh company-specific earnings warning but MWC's cancellation mattered because it was a major launch customer and dealmaking venue for the mobile industry. That plus concern about handset demand and Asian supply chains likely drove the selloff.

primary_cause: Commercial-aerospace exposure through UTC as investors repriced airline/travel weakness
secondary_factors: Broad defense/aerospace and industrial selling
store_description: RTX's larger decline versus Lockheed makes sense because investors were not just selling defense they were also selling commercial aerospace. As the virus spread and travel demand came under threat the UTC side of the merged company made RTX more economically exposed than pure-defense peers.

primary_cause: Collapsing rate expectations threatening net interest revenue. Treasury yields hit record lows
secondary_factors: Broad financial-sector liquidation and recession fears
store_description: Schwab's business model made it especially vulnerable to the violent move in rates. Falling yields and expected Fed easing directly pressure client-cash spread income so this was more than just a generic bank selloff even though there was no fresh Schwab headline.

primary_cause: Physical-retail/foot-traffic risk from COVID-19
secondary_factors: REIT de-risking and discretionary retail weakness
store_description: Simon's move looks fundamentally tied to the market realizing that enclosed malls are highly exposed to any outbreak-driven drop in traffic. Even before formal shutdowns investors were already discounting lower shopper visits weaker tenant sales and tourism exposure.

primary_cause: No clear stock-specific catalyst. Broad healthcare/life-science tools selloff
secondary_factors: Despite developing COVID tests. General de-risking and uncertainty over biopharma/lab activity
store_description: Thermo Fisher's drop does not appear to reflect a negative company announcement. Despite some potential testing upside investors on Feb. 25 were broadly selling high-quality growth and healthcare-equipment names as the market prioritized immediate macro risk over longer-term opportunity.

primary_cause: China production and demand disruption. Tesla warned Shanghai Model 3 ramp delayed 1-1.5 weeks
secondary_factors: Valuation-sensitive momentum unwind and broad market selloff. Feb China car sales plunged ~80%
store_description: Tesla had a real virus-specific operational issue. Shanghai production and deliveries were disrupted and the Chinese auto market was collapsing. By Feb. 25 the stock was still highly momentum-driven so the broader risk-off tape likely compounded a name-specific China shock.

primary_cause: Travel/mobility demand shock from COVID-19
secondary_factors: General high-beta growth selloff
store_description: Uber's drop looks primarily thematic. The market quickly moved to price lower ride demand fewer airport trips and weaker urban activity if the outbreak widened. No better stock-specific headline found so the simplest explanation is that Uber was one of the clearest COVID-exposed consumer platforms.

primary_cause: No clear UNH-specific catalyst. COVID-driven uncertainty around healthcare utilization/costs
secondary_factors: Broad defensive rotation failing because even healthcare was being de-risked
store_description: UnitedHealth's selloff does not appear linked to a company announcement. Insurers were caught in the general repricing of healthcare-system risk once U.S. community spread looked likely with investors unsure whether near-term utilization and costs would be favorable or adverse.

primary_cause: Freight-volume fears from supply-chain disruption and slowing trade
secondary_factors: Broader industrial/recession scare. Reuters Feb 6: China outbreak disrupting container shipping
store_description: Union Pacific's move fits the transportation macro. If China-related shipping and production were disrupted rail volumes were likely next in line. The trade/freight slowdown narrative was already clearly in motion.

primary_cause: Global shipping/logistics disruption fears from COVID-19
secondary_factors: Broader transport-sector selloff and recession fears. Reuters: container shipping out of sync
store_description: UPS appears to have sold off on concern that global package and freight networks would be disrupted as the virus spread and Asian trade flows weakened. Logistics exposure to a sudden growth shock is the most likely explanation.
